tolerance.note: logic may drift a few percent with synthesis changes, but BSRAM and DSP counts are structural and must be exact; fmax must stay within 3% and above 25 MHz

runtime.note: loader-only: blank RAM, immutable UART ROM, no baked program. This is the bitstream a board should be running, and the one every shipped payload (games, examples, kernels) executes on, so it is locked instead of a per-program row. It used to cost about 1,534 LUT4 more than a baked image because axrom read combinationally and could not map to BSRAM; with axrom's SYNC_READ it is now 457 LUT4 *below* the baked `cpu` row it replaces (13,387 against 13,844 in this same sweep), for 2 of the ~20 spare BSRAMs and 0.55 MHz. Decoupling a profile from its payload is now the cheaper option, not a cost.

ax2.note: Known failure, and a deliberate one: `core.ax2` is a profile for a larger part than this one, kept here so the Primer records how far over it is rather than pretending it is a Primer design. It needs 25,569 LUT4 against 23,040 (111%), so no seed or placer effort can help -- unlike `runtime-tpu`, which fits and merely places badly. Measured by parameter, the 64-entry BTB costs 5,820 LUT-family cells and the second issue slot 8,086, over a 19,286-cell single-issue baseline. The BTB is 64 x 60 = 3,840 bits read combinationally at two indices with a write port, so it becomes a LUT register file at ~1.5 cells/bit, and it cannot take the SYNC_READ treatment that moved axram and axrom into BSRAM: ax2_icache.sv needs the lookup combinational to steer the *next* fetch, and registering it costs the bubble the predictor exists to avoid. Making it fit on this device means dropping branch prediction, which changes what the profile measures -- so measure AX2 on a larger board instead. A build that starts passing is also a baseline violation and must be re-locked deliberately.

runtime-ax2.note: Loader form of the ax2 profile: identical hardware, reset into the ROM, blank RAM, no baked program. Fails for the same reason `ax2` does -- the part is too small for a dual-issue core with a 64-entry BTB, not anything about the loader -- confirmed by building it, not assumed. Recorded rather than dropped so the pair stays comparable and so a build that starts passing is a deliberate re-lock. The decoupling itself is proven on every other Primer profile; this one waits on a larger board.

runtime-gpu4.note: loader form of the 4-lane minimal-host GPU profile (`-runtime-gpu` is a different machine: reference core, one lane, 32 KiB). Payload budget is 16384-4096 = 12 KiB.

runtime-tpu.note: loader form of the TPU profile. PLACEMENT-FRAGILE: it fits comfortably (80% LUT4, 89% BSRAM, 24/56 DSP) but legalises on only one seed in five -- measured FAIL/PASS/FAIL/FAIL/FAIL for seeds 1-5 -- so the profile pins `pnr_seed: 2` the way `-runtime-gpu` pins 3. Nothing is over capacity; what is scarce is placement freedom, because 50 block RAMs and 24 multipliers must land in fixed GW5A columns and the boot ROM adds the last 2 BSRAMs on top of baked `tpu`'s 48. Treat a failure here as a re-roll of the analytic placer, not a size regression, and re-seed rather than shrink -- but do not assume the pinned seed survives an unrelated RTL change, because any netlist edit re-rolls it. The loader costs +766 LUT4 and +2 BSRAM over baked `tpu`, and routes 1.01 MHz faster.

provenance.note: Ten rows come from the 11-profile sweep tangprimer25k-synth-2026-08-12.json. `runtime-tpu` is re-locked from its own later single-profile run because the main sweep predates pinning `pnr_seed: 2` in its config and therefore recorded it failing at seed 1. Checking the lock against the main sweep alone will flag `runtime-tpu` for that reason and no other; the next full sweep will cover all eleven coherently.
